pages.title: Documentation plan
pages.question: Where should I start, and which page answers the task I have now?
pages.brief: This page will map the path from understanding one shop order to running a checked NeoHaskell project and building a feature with an agent. It will link directly to installation, project creation, the first response, and setup recovery, alongside the tutorial and concrete task guides. Short descriptions will distinguish existing articles from planned coverage and help returning readers find the appropriate reference without repeating the entire sidebar.

pages.title: Core concepts
pages.question: What does an application do when an order is accepted or rejected?
pages.brief: This page will continue to introduce commands, decisions, events, and queries through a shop selling ceramic mugs. Readers will follow one accepted order and one rejected order, predict remaining stock, and distinguish the event history from the query result. The existing tables and plain-text examples will remain. A compact static figure may connect the four concepts before readers continue to installation or model their own first feature.

pages.title: Install NeoHaskell
pages.question: What must be installed, and how can I tell the toolchain is available?
pages.brief: This page will identify the supported environment and install the Neo CLI with its required Nix and Git tools. It will distinguish installing the CLI from obtaining the project-managed compiler and libraries, explain the optional editor environment, and show checks for the installed tools. Instructions will be tied to a verified release and platform, with binary-cache choices explained where they affect the first build and direct links to setup recovery.

pages.title: Create a project
pages.question: Where do I run project creation, and what will it produce?
pages.brief: This page will create a named application with the Neo CLI, explain where to run the command, and identify the Counter starter that appears in the new directory. It will show the ordinary interactive route and a reproducible command for an agent, explain the initial Git commit and framework pin, and confirm the generated project before continuing. Library creation and the full set of CLI options will remain reference topics.

pages.title: Run the application
pages.question: How do I start and stop the starter, and which terminal must remain open?
pages.brief: This page will build and run the generated Counter application from its project root, identify the local HTTP address, and explain which process must remain running while requests are sent from another terminal. It will distinguish an initial dependency download from application startup, show how to stop and restart the process, and explain that the default in-memory event history disappears when the process ends. Watch mode will be introduced only after the first successful launch.

pages.title: Check your first response
pages.question: Is the application actually processing commands and answering queries?
pages.brief: This page will verify the running starter by creating a Counter, using the returned entity identifier in a change command, and reading the resulting value through its query. It will explain the request payload, response envelope, and possible delay before the projection reflects the change. A rejected input will distinguish a working validation response from a setup failure. The maintained Counter scenario will provide a repeatable check before readers begin the shop tutorial.

pages.title: Find your project files
pages.question: Which file owns the behavior, wiring, configuration, and evidence I am reviewing?
pages.brief: This page will map the generated project to the decisions a reader and their agent need to make. It will locate the application Event Model, the Counter feature, command decisions, events, entity updates, queries, and tests, then distinguish those authored files from build files regenerated from neo.json. A compact directory map will connect each location to its purpose. Readers will learn where to inspect a proposed change without studying every framework module.

pages.title: Set up your agent
pages.question: How does my coding agent get the project conventions, and what should I ask it to do first?
pages.brief: This page will retain its existing agent installation guidance, shop task, and accepted-versus-rejected checks while linking environment preparation and first-run work to dedicated pages. It will distinguish shared workflow skills from guidance matched to the application's framework revision, explain the supported agent choices for the documented CLI version, and verify the installed instructions in the project. The first request will remain small enough for the reader to judge before entering the application tutorial.

pages.title: Fix setup problems
pages.question: Which setup step failed, and what is the smallest safe correction?
pages.brief: This page will connect common first-run symptoms to the failed step and its smallest corrective action: missing tools, the wrong working directory, an existing project name, invalid project configuration, unavailable dependencies, or missing agent guidance. Each case will show a verified diagnostic and the check that confirms recovery. It will preserve the reader's files, explain how to identify their CLI and framework versions, and link deeper compiler or runtime errors to the reference.

pages.title: Plan the mug shop
pages.question: What must our one-mug order do?
pages.brief: This page will specify a shop that starts with three ceramic mugs and accepts an order for one mug only while stock remains. Readers will predict the command, decision, recorded event, and stock query for accepted and sold-out cases. A small behavior table will become the acceptance criteria handed to the agent. The page will also distinguish the illustration's supplied opening stock from the initialization the implemented application must perform.

pages.title: Create the shop feature
pages.question: Where do the shop state and events belong?
pages.brief: This page will continue from the working project produced by setup, inspect the generated Counter files, and give an agent the bounded task of introducing the shop's state and events. An annotated file tree will explain Entity, Event, Core, and Feature without teaching every import. Readers will establish opening stock explicitly and inspect how an accepted order changes it. The proposed shop identifiers will be verified before any runnable source is published.

pages.title: Accept or reject an order
pages.question: When should the shop accept or reject an order?
pages.brief: This page will implement the shop's one-mug decision using the current command shape, entity lookup, and explicit accept or reject result. Readers will follow an available-stock case and a sold-out case through the same function, then connect only accepted orders to recorded events. Short source excerpts beside the two outcomes will explain the syntax needed at that point. Missing shop state will receive its own rejection case, without introducing transport or payment behavior.

pages.title: Query available stock
pages.question: How do I read the remaining stock?
pages.brief: This page will turn the shop's current state into a stock query and show why its answer is separate from the event history. Readers will follow one accepted order from three mugs to two, then verify that a rejected order changes neither history nor stock. A compact history-and-answer figure will accompany the projection code and its declared event inputs. The lesson will explain that the HTTP query may need time to reflect an accepted command.

pages.title: Place an order over HTTP
pages.question: How can I place an order through the running service?
pages.brief: This page will register the shop's command and query through its Feature and compose that Feature into the application's named Event Model. Readers will send one accepted order and one rejected order, then inspect the stock query through the running HTTP service. A focused wiring excerpt and adjacent request-and-response pairs will connect source to observable behavior. The tutorial will use verified shop routes and payloads, with broader HTTP and MCP choices linked to their task guide.

pages.title: Test shop behavior
pages.question: What checks show that the shop behaves as specified?
pages.brief: This page will turn the original shop table into repeatable checks for an accepted order, sold-out rejection, missing shop state, and the resulting stock query. Readers will distinguish a decision test from an event replay check and an HTTP scenario, then inspect one intentional failure and its repair. Expected and observed results will appear together. The agent's evidence must include the actual checks run and account for delayed query updates rather than assuming immediate consistency.

pages.title: Keep one mug in reserve
pages.question: How can I change the stock policy without breaking existing behavior?
pages.brief: This page will ask the agent to change the shop so that one mug remains available for in-person sales. Readers will update the behavior table first, inspect the decision diff, and check the new boundary alongside existing accepted and rejected orders. A before-and-after comparison will show which outcome intentionally changes and which must remain stable. The lesson will finish with reviewed source and check results, then link to the reusable agent workflow guide.

pages.title: Work with an AI agent
pages.question: How do I request and verify a bounded application change?
pages.brief: This page will turn a behavior request into a bounded agent task with the project revision, relevant source, acceptance cases, and permitted changes. It will show a reusable prompt and a focused diff, then compare the requested outcome with decision tests and interface evidence. A correction example will distinguish a compiler success from correct behavior and direct the agent to the maintained guidance for the pinned framework.
pages.boundary: Setup owns installation; tutorial owns the first worked change; this guide owns repeating and correcting the process.

pages.title: Expose an HTTP API
pages.question: How do I call my commands and queries over HTTP?
pages.brief: This page will expose an existing feature through the Web transport and inspect its generated routes and OpenAPI contract. A command request, rejected input, and query response will connect the application definition to observable HTTP behavior. Filtering and pagination will follow the [query contract](/reference/framework/queries/). The examples will include transport registration and browser-origin configuration, then link to authentication before opening the interface to untrusted callers.

evidence.symbol: OpenAPI routes and WAI application assembly

pages.boundary: Keep the existing route as the first focused transport task. Reference owns every field and status mapping; tutorial owns building the feature.

pages.title: Expose MCP tools and resources
pages.question: How can an agent call this application through MCP?
pages.brief: This page will register the stdio MCP transport for an existing feature and show initialization, tool discovery, a command call, and reading a query resource. A compact protocol transcript will distinguish commands as tools from queries as resources. The example will explain process ownership and the trusted execution context so readers do not mistake this local protocol for an authenticated remote HTTP service.
pages.boundary: Reference owns protocol structures. This page owns wiring and exercising the local process, not remote MCP hosting.

pages.title: Run commands from a terminal
pages.question: How do I invoke my application behavior from a terminal?
pages.brief: This page will register the application CLI transport and invoke a command using the generated entity and command grouping. It will pair terminal inputs with successful and rejected outcomes and explain how output mode affects scripting. The example will identify the local operator trust boundary and distinguish this application interface from the neo development CLI used to create and manage a project.
pages.boundary: The neo CLI reference owns development commands. This guide owns the application executable interface.

pages.title: Keep events across restarts
pages.question: How do I keep recorded application history when the process stops?
pages.brief: This page will replace the starter memory configuration with a persistent event store and verify the same recorded behavior before and after a restart. A comparison will distinguish SimpleEventStore disk persistence from PostgreSQL configuration, while a diagram separates event history from derived query state. The example will use a complete configuration for the selected framework revision and explain which storage paths or database volumes must survive.
pages.boundary: Concepts explains history versus state; reference lists settings; this page owns an event persistence change and restart check.

pages.title: Persist and rebuild queries
pages.question: How do query results recover after a restart or projection change?
pages.brief: This page will configure persistent query storage separately from event history and follow checkpoint resume and an explicitly verified rebuild. It will explain that the current query hash is derived from the query name, so changing projection code alone does not automatically invalidate saved progress. A timeline will show live events arriving during replay and when readiness becomes available. A rebuild failure will connect diagnostic evidence to recovery, which depends on usable history and does not reverse external effects.
pages.boundary: Concepts owns why derived state exists; this guide owns configuration and recovery. Link checkpoint reference rather than reproduce its API.

pages.title: Upload and retrieve files
pages.question: How do I attach a user file and restrict its retrieval?
pages.brief: This page will configure file metadata and blob storage, upload a document, attach its file reference to a command, and retrieve it as its owner. A sequence will distinguish pending uploads, confirmed attachments, expiration, and missing blobs. Paired requests will demonstrate permitted and denied retrieval, while the persistence discussion will keep the file bytes, ownership metadata, and application events separate.
pages.boundary: Access guides own general identity and policies; storage owns events; this page owns the uploaded-file lifecycle.

pages.title: Generate a document
pages.question: How do I keep a server-generated file for its owner?
pages.brief: This page will follow a document request through an outbound handler that generates bytes, stores an owned retained file, and emits a command recording its reference. A retry example will reuse a stable creation key and compare matching content with a conflicting attempt. The figure will distinguish retained documents from pending uploads and show why both the blob directory and file metadata need durable storage.
pages.boundary: Integrations owns generic outbound effects; this page owns retained file creation and its idempotency boundary. Adapt upstream let-in syntax to approved do blocks when teaching code is authored.

pages.title: Erase a protected value
pages.question: How do I make an owned protected value unreadable without deleting history?
pages.brief: This page will introduce a narrowly scoped erasure task using the PostgreSQL-backed protected-value mechanism. It will follow an authorized owner request, deletion of one protected reference, the resulting command, and an explicit retry. A before-and-after figure will distinguish the retained event record from the unavailable protected content, and explain how queries and external copies must be considered separately when checking the intended outcome.
pages.boundary: This is a specific task, not a claim of regulatory compliance or arbitrary event deletion. Concepts owns the historical model.

pages.title: Verify caller identity
pages.question: How does my HTTP application recognize a caller?
pages.brief: This page will connect an application to an OIDC issuer, configure the expected token audience where required, and inspect the user claims available to a command. A request comparison will cover a valid token, an invalid token, and an anonymous caller. A small boundary figure will separate identity verification from command permission and from connecting the caller to an external OAuth provider.
pages.boundary: This guide owns inbound JWT identity configuration. Authorization owns permission and resource ownership; external connections own provider tokens.

pages.title: Authorize a command
pages.question: Who may run this command against this entity?
pages.brief: This page will protect one command with a declared access policy and a decision that checks the relevant entity ownership. A table will compare anonymous callers, authenticated owners, other users, and a trusted local invocation. The accompanying tests will verify that denied commands do not reach the decision or append events, and show why enabling authentication is necessary for the HTTP policy gate to apply.
pages.boundary: Retain the old route as the first permission task. Identity setup remains separate; reference owns policy helper signatures.

pages.title: Restrict query results
pages.question: Who may read a query and its individual results?
pages.brief: This page will apply a query-level access check before fetching data and an ownership check for individual results. It will compare the same query for an owner, another authenticated user, and an anonymous caller, including a paginated result. A short decision table will show where each check runs so a reader can protect returned data without assuming that command permissions automatically protect query endpoints.
pages.boundary: Reference owns query and pagination APIs; this guide owns the access scenario and verification.

pages.title: Call an external service
pages.question: How do I perform an external effect after a decision?
pages.brief: This page will connect an accepted event to a typed outbound handler, perform an HTTP call, and turn the provider response into a follow-up command. Success and failure traces will show the boundary between a pure decision and an external effect. The example will use an idempotency key and explain the separate HTTP and dispatcher retry settings, without promising durable delivery or exactly-once execution.
pages.boundary: Retain the old route as first outbound task. Concepts owns purity; reference owns typed action and retry options.

pages.title: Run an inbound worker
pages.question: How can a background source send typed application commands?
pages.brief: This page will register a typed inbound worker that emits commands to declared entity targets. A small timer-driven example will show the worker configuration, supported command set, and application wiring, followed by a rejected target at compilation. A lifecycle figure will identify startup and stopping responsibilities, while the prose distinguishes a long-running inbound source from an outbound reaction to an accepted event.
pages.boundary: Reference owns type machinery. This guide owns connecting a bounded background source, not a generic job queue guarantee.

pages.title: Connect an external account
pages.question: How does a user authorize access to a provider account?
pages.brief: This page will register an OAuth provider and follow an authenticated user through connect, callback, token use, refresh, and disconnect. A sequence diagram will separate the application identity from provider credentials and temporary connection state. It will explain the consumer-supplied persistent secret store and the current in-memory callback transaction store, including what happens to an unfinished connection after a restart or a request reaches another instance.
pages.boundary: Authentication owns application identity; this page owns provider consent and credentials. Configuration reference owns provider fields.

pages.title: Deploy an application
pages.question: What must be configured and persisted to run this application elsewhere?
pages.brief: This page will assemble a reproducible deployment example for a pinned application and framework revision, naming the executable, runtime configuration, database, and file paths. A deployment figure will distinguish persistent services from the application process and show the public HTTP boundary. Verification will cover startup, an accepted command, a query, and a restart, while identifying environment-specific hosting and process supervision that the repository does not supply.

evidence.symbol: pinned framework input and project flake

pages.boundary: Reference owns all configuration values; setup owns local installation. The compose file provisions PostgreSQL, not a complete hosted application deployment.

pages.title: Check readiness and failures
pages.question: How do I tell whether the application is ready and locate a failed operation?
pages.brief: This page will compare the health endpoint with query readiness and follow a failed operation using its request identifier and structured logs. A small state diagram will show rebuilding, ready, and failed query states alongside their HTTP results. Worked diagnostics will distinguish a storage failure from an unavailable integration, and connect recovery steps to evidence rather than treating a running process as proof that every query is usable.
pages.boundary: Errors reference owns a searchable symptom catalog; this guide owns the operating procedure and readiness interpretation.

pages.title: Features, chapters, and slices
pages.question: How does an application story become a model that stays connected to its implementation?
pages.brief: This page will explain how an Event Model groups application behavior into features, chapters, and slices, and why each slice has a focused responsibility. An annotated Counter feature tree will connect a command slice and a query slice to their declared events. It will contrast organizing a story with enforcing an entity boundary, then link to the tutorial for implementation and framework reference for the DSL.

pages.title: Commands, decisions, and outcomes
pages.question: What can happen when a command reaches the application?
pages.brief: This page will follow a stock reservation from intention to domain decision and persistence. A compact outcome table will distinguish acceptance with one or several events, acceptance without events, domain rejection, and execution failure. It will explain why rejecting insufficient stock differs from failing to save an accepted change. The first shop illustration will remain a deliberately small case, with links to testing and troubleshooting for procedures.

pages.title: Entities and event streams
pages.question: Which facts must a decision consider together, and what happens when commands compete?
pages.brief: This page will explain an entity as state reconstructed from one identified event stream and as the boundary within which a command checks its conditions. Two competing stock reservations will illustrate a stale decision, an append conflict, and evaluation against refreshed state. A two-lane sequence figure will keep cart and stock histories separate. It will explain the boundary without promising an atomic transaction across both entities.

pages.title: History and current state
pages.question: Why retain events when the application already has current state?
pages.brief: This page will distinguish the facts recorded in an event stream from the entity state obtained by applying them in order. An aligned Counter ledger and state table will show how the same history reconstructs the same entity through its update function. It will explain that replay derives state from recorded facts rather than rerunning original commands, and hand query rebuilding to its own page and persistence setup to the storage guide.

pages.title: Query projections and replay
pages.question: How can the same history answer different questions, and how does a query catch up?
pages.brief: This page will explain query state as a separately maintained answer derived from selected event sources. The cart and stock activity query will show that a query can combine entities without merging their command boundaries. A diagram will separate event history, projection updates, and persisted checkpoint position. It will compare resuming compatible progress with rebuilding changed query state, including readiness during replay, without turning the explanation into a recovery runbook.

pages.title: Pure decisions and effects
pages.question: What does purity mean when a decision needs context or generated values?
pages.brief: This page will separate constructing a decision from interpreting it and performing effects. A boundary figure will place command data, current entity state, and request context beside the decision description, with UUID generation and protected-value operations in the interpreter. It will explain which inputs must be controlled for repeatable tests and why purity does not prove the intended business behavior. Network integrations will lead to the workflow explanation and task guide.

pages.title: Workflows across entities
pages.question: How does one recorded fact cause another part of the application to act?
pages.brief: This page will explain how outbound integrations react to recorded events and issue commands to another entity, while inbound integrations introduce commands from outside. The existing cart-to-stock declaration will provide a small sequence figure with two separate decisions and histories. The explanation will identify where later work can fail and why an earlier event remains a fact. Provider configuration and retry procedures will stay in the integration guide.

pages.title: Identity and permissions
pages.question: Why does knowing who someone is not decide what they may do or read?
pages.brief: This page will separate authenticated identity, permission to invoke an operation, ownership of particular data, and domain acceptance. A small comparison table will trace the same signed-in user through an allowed query, a forbidden record, and a rejected business command. It will explain request context and the distinct query access and instance checks, while leaving provider setup, policy implementation, and endpoint testing to the access-control guide.

pages.title: Syntax and expressions
pages.question: What does this expression mean?
pages.brief: This page will make everyday source readable through modules and imports, function application, signatures, pipelines, record access, conditionals, case expressions, and do blocks. Each construct will get one compact source and result pair, with stable anchors for tutorial links. It will explain qualified operations and generated language extensions, using let statements inside do blocks for local bindings and linking type definitions to the next page.

pages.title: Types and records
pages.question: How do I read or define the shapes in a feature?
pages.brief: This page will cover type parameters, records, constructors, sum types, type aliases, class constraints, associated types, visible type application, and deriving notation as they appear in application code. A compact annotated command record and event sum will connect source spelling to possible values. It will distinguish handwritten definitions from derive helpers, with links to framework contracts instead of teaching metaprogramming or reproducing a Haskell language manual.

pages.title: Values and common types
pages.question: Which types and operations are already available through Core?
pages.brief: This page will serve as the Core entry point and scalar lookup: Text, numeric types, Bool, Unit, Uuid, and the difference between a re-exported type and qualified module operations. A short type-to-module table will route readers to containers, optional results, tasks, and JSON. Selected signatures will show text conversion and arithmetic conventions; advanced concurrency and implementation modules will remain linked source rather than fill the sidebar.

evidence.symbol: Basics numeric, Boolean and comparison exports

pages.title: Arrays and maps
pages.question: How do I transform a collection or look up an item?
pages.brief: This page will group Array and Map operations by constructing, finding, transforming, combining, and reducing data. Signature tables will make pipeline argument order explicit, while small examples will show an absent index or key, empty collections, and a simple total. Related operations will have anchors on one page, with linked canonical definitions and edge cases, rather than a separate route for every exported function.

pages.title: Maybe and Result
pages.question: How do I represent absence or a recoverable failure?
pages.brief: This page will compare Nothing and Just with Err and Ok, showing when absence carries no explanation and when a typed error is needed. Compact signatures and paired cases will cover map, andThen, withDefault, mapError, and conversions between the two containers. A parsing or lookup example will retain the error until the caller deliberately handles it, and link effectful failure handling to Task.

pages.title: Tasks and effects
pages.question: How do I sequence work that can fail?
pages.brief: This page will document Task error value, successful construction, typed failure, chaining, do notation, recovery, and conversion to Result. One short sequence will show which step runs and what happens after failure; a signature table will separate constructing a task from executing it at the program boundary. Cleanup and cancellation will be linked advanced entries, with Decision explicitly cross-linked as the separate contract for business acceptance and rejection.

pages.title: JSON and schemas
pages.question: How do typed values become JSON and API schemas?
pages.brief: This page will cover Json encoding and decoding, FromJSON and ToJSON instances, malformed input as Result, and the separate Schema contract used to describe API data. A small record will be paired with its JSON shape and one invalid input. It will distinguish serialization from validation and generated API descriptions, keeping parser helpers in anchored tables and linking command payload details to the transport reference.

pages.title: Event models and features
pages.question: How do the declared features become a running application?
pages.brief: This page will map EventModel, FeatureAction, chapter, slice, entity, command, produces, query, and readsFrom to the source-local Counter feature. A compact relationship figure will show declaration, validation, and runtime assembly without mixing event history with query rows. Builder signatures and ordering constraints will sit beside the model. Direct Service.Application assembly will be a linked advanced section, preserving its public status while leading with the current starter architecture.

pages.title: Commands and decisions
pages.question: What must a command define, and what can a decision return?
pages.brief: This page will specify the command record, EntityOf, getEntityId, decide, RequestContext, transport permissions, and derivation helpers, mapping authored functions to public Command methods. It will compare acceptNew, acceptExisting, acceptAny, acceptAfter, and reject through a compact outcome table. Counter decision cases will ground accepted and rejected behavior. Multi-tenant signatures and authorization hooks will have anchors, with task guides owning the longer implementation and access-policy walkthroughs.

pages.title: Entities and events
pages.question: How is an entity identified and rebuilt from its events?
pages.brief: This page will specify EntityOf, EventOf, EntityIdType, initialState, update, event routing, and the relevant derive helpers. A short event sequence and successive entity states will show the pure fold, while signatures make argument order and stream identity explicit. It will explain the distinction between a single event payload and the entity event sum, linking persistence settings and compatibility changes to their task guides.

pages.title: Queries and projections
pages.question: What updates a query row, and what may a caller read?
pages.brief: This page will define Query, QueryOf, EntitiesOf, queryId, combine, and the Update, Delete, and NoOp outcomes. A small entity-to-query example will show row identity separately from event stream identity. Anchored sections will cover NeoQL filtering, pagination inputs and response fields, result limits, pre-fetch access, and per-row visibility. The Counter query will supply the concrete consumer, with links to HTTP requests, storage, and authorization tasks instead of repeating their complete procedures.

pages.title: Transport contracts
pages.question: What interface does a registered command or query expose?
pages.brief: This page will compare Web, application CLI, and MCP registration, showing that a command must allow its transport and the model must install it. It will record route naming, command responses, query handler inputs, and schema registration with one request and response shape. An advanced anchored section will describe the public Transport interface. The application CLI will be clearly distinguished from the neo development command reference.

evidence.symbol: Maintained Web, CLI and MCP contracts

pages.title: Neo commands
pages.question: Which command and flags do I need for local development?
pages.brief: This page will document neo new, build, run, test, and lock, with invocation, working directory, inputs, flags, and source-defined outcomes in a compact command table. Global verbose and CI options, watch behavior, library creation, and the build lock check will have anchors. It will link model tools and agent setup commands to their own bounded pages, while installation and the complete first launch remain in getting started.

pages.title: IDE, inspect, and validate
pages.question: How do I inspect or validate the model from the command line?
pages.brief: This page will list neo ide host and port settings, inspect filters, inspect sync, and validate path and JSON options. A compact table will distinguish read-only inspection from source-to-model synchronization and IDE edits. It will record validation exit codes and show the structure of a future captured result, linking model-authoring tasks elsewhere. Command contracts will be tied to the documented revision rather than assumed present in older binaries.

pages.title: Skills and agent guidance
pages.question: How do I select installed skills and refresh matching API guidance?
pages.brief: This page will document neo skills setup tool selection, skill filtering, all-tools, force, dry-run, and refresh options, plus neo guidance retry. It will distinguish shared workflow skills from source-matched framework guidance synchronized by build, run, and test. A concise destination and option table will explain what is written and preserved. Longer agent onboarding stays in its guide, and no generic feature-generation command will be implied.

pages.title: Runtime configuration
pages.question: Which value wins when defaults, environment, and arguments disagree?
pages.brief: This page will define Config fields, required documentation, defaults, required values, environment names, command flags, nested records, and secret redaction. A single precedence table will show command line, process environment, dotenv, then default, with a small hypothetical port example. It will explain startup loading, configuration factories, registration order, and separate store choices, linking provider-specific settings to task guides and keeping neo.json build configuration on its own page.

pages.title: neo.json and dependencies
pages.question: Which project settings control generated build files and framework versions?
pages.brief: This page will describe neo.json name, version, neo-version, project type, metadata, license default, and dependency entries, separating these from runtime environment settings. A small complete manifest and field table will explain generated Cabal and Nix ownership and link supported dependency forms. A source-selection section will identify the local framework override as an advanced development setting, while release compatibility remains explicit rather than equating main with a published version.

Internal local framework source override validation

pages.title: Setup and build errors
pages.question: Why did the development command fail, and what should I check next?
pages.brief: This page will index observable failures such as a missing workspace, invalid neo.json, missing prerequisites, invalid dependencies, unavailable framework guidance, and failed child processes. Entries will pair the diagnostic code and location with the smallest correction and a recovery check. One annotated diagnostic will explain source spans and retained child output. Source-defined messages will stay distinct from executed transcripts, with links to CLI options and community reporting when correction needs more evidence.

evidence.symbol: NeoError workspace, config and prerequisite diagnostics

pages.title: Startup and request errors
pages.question: Was the failure configuration, access, a business rejection, or infrastructure?
pages.brief: This page will separate startup configuration failures, invalid bind settings, occupied listeners, command rejection, authorization denial, and execution failure. A compact symptom table will connect each category to the responsible configuration or public response type and one recovery check. It will show why a rejected command is a valid business outcome, not automatically a server defect, and route store or provider failures to their maintained task guidance.

evidence.symbol: Decision rejection cases inspected, not run

pages.title: Resources and project status
pages.question: Where do I find maintained instructions, version history, and help?
pages.brief: This page will retain its existing substantive setup, source, storage, authorization, license, release, and community guidance while linking the more precise reference destinations. Its upstream links will remain tied to the revision they describe, with current-main research kept separate from published releases and agent-skills versions. A compact compatibility table may be added once versions are verified; no new support commitment or runtime verification claim will be invented.

decisions: 61 destinations: retain all 24 existing routes and add 37 focused page briefs.
Keep Start here and the seven-chapter tutorial flat. Use one subgroup level for the larger task and reference sections. Concepts remain eight related explanations.
Native Starlight disclosures remain collapsed except the current branch. Expand no deeper than section, subgroup, page.
The first planned sequence becomes concepts, installation, creation, launch, response, project files, agent setup. The existing direct concepts-to-agent link stays in substantive prose.
Preserve the three existing substantive articles and their executable or illustrative examples; only their final planning paragraphs and pagination change.
Keep the map explicitly titled Documentation plan, internally searchable and externally noindexed. All other standalone plans stay excluded from both indexes.
